chapters.title: Chapter 5: From Paper Valuation to Real Money

lessons.title: Headline Valuation vs What Your Stake Is Actually Worth

children.text: A startup you backed announces a round at a ₹400 crore valuation. You own 0.5%. The maths feels obvious: your stake is worth ₹2 crore. Friends congratulate you, and you start mentally spending it. But that ₹2 crore is not a price anyone will pay you today, and it may be far above what you ever receive. This lesson breaks down the gap between the headline number and the realistic value of your shares, and gives you a simple method to estimate what your stake is actually worth.

body.text: Headline valuation × your percentage is the most optimistic number you will ever see for your stake. It ignores what sits ahead of you, how long you must wait, the chance of getting there and the fact that nobody may buy your shares today.

children.text: What the Headline Number Assumes

columns.label: What the headline assumes
points: Every share is worth the latest round price
Equity shares are worth the same as CCPS with preference
You could sell today at that price
The company will reach an exit at least that large
Money today and money in six years are the same
No tax, fees or carried interest

columns.label: What is actually true
points: The round price was paid by one investor for one instrument
CCPS carry liquidation preference and protections equity lacks
There is usually no buyer, or only one at a steep discount
Many startups exit below their last valuation or not at all
Money years away is worth less today
Tax, fund fees and carry reduce what reaches you

children.text: Five Gaps Between Paper and Pocket
The instrument gap.

The round price was set for CCPS with a liquidation preference. Your plain equity shares, without those rights, are worth less. That is also why independent fair market value reports for equity shares often come in below the round price.
The preference gap.
In any sale below a certain value, preference holders are paid first. Equity holders share only what is left.
The liquidity gap.
There is no exchange for your shares. A secondary buyer, if one exists, will usually demand a discount for tying up money in an asset they cannot easily sell.
The time and risk gap.
An exit may be five to seven years away, and it may never happen. Future money must be discounted for both waiting and uncertainty.
The tax and fees gap.
Capital gains tax, and carried interest and fees if you invested through a fund or syndicate, all come out before the money reaches your bank account.
Worked Example: Meenakshi's ₹2 Crore Stake

UrbanNest Coliving Private Limited is a fictional Pune startup running managed hostels for young professionals. Meenakshi, a Pune chartered accountant, invested ₹20 lakh in its seed round through equity shares. She now owns 0.5% on a fully diluted basis. UrbanNest's latest round valued it at ₹400 crore post-money.

Instead of assuming one outcome, estimate a few realistic exits over the next six years and what Meenakshi receives in each. Assume no debt, and that CCPS holders either take their preference or convert, whichever gives them more, treated as one group.

body.caption: Four possible futures for UrbanNest in six years (illustrative)

cells: Convert: 45% × ₹1,500 crore = ₹675 crore, more than ₹180 crore
Take preference: ₹180 crore, more than 45% × ₹300 crore = ₹135 crore
₹120 crore left for the other 55%; her share: 0.5 ÷ 55 × ₹120 crore = ₹1.09 crore
Take all ₹100 crore, less than their ₹180 crore preference

body.title: What Meenakshi receives in each outcome (₹ lakh)

body.text: Look at the modest sale. UrbanNest sells for ₹300 crore, only 25% below its last valuation, yet Meenakshi receives ₹1.09 crore, 45% below her ₹2 crore headline. The ₹180 crore preference takes a bigger bite out of equity holders than the fall in valuation alone.

Step 2: Discount back to today
Money in six years, with this much risk, is worth much less today. Using a 25% annual discount rate, a reasonable hurdle for a late-stage private investment:

body.caption: A rough estimate of what the stake is worth today

children.text: That does not make Meenakshi's investment a failure. A realistic 2.4x today, with a 20% chance of a ₹7.5 crore outcome, is a strong early-stage result. It simply is not ₹2 crore, and she should not plan her finances as if it were.

body.text: Every input here is an assumption: the probabilities, the exit values, the discount rate and the treatment of preferences. Change them and the answer moves. The point is not precision. It is to replace one flattering number with a range you can actually reason about.

body.title: Your share of a sale below the headline
body.prompt: A startup last valued at ₹200 crore is sold for ₹90 crore. It has ₹50 crore of 1x non-participating CCPS preference. The CCPS holders own 40% on an as-converted basis. You hold 1.2% of the company through equity shares. How much do you receive, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: Converting would give CCPS holders 40% × ₹90 crore = ₹36 crore, less than their ₹50 crore preference, so they take ₹50 crore. That leaves ₹40 crore for the remaining 60%. Your share = 1.2 ÷ 60 × ₹40 crore = ₹0.8 crore, or ₹80 lakh. The headline value of your stake was 1.2% × ₹200 crore = ₹2.4 crore.

children.text: The Liquidity Gap: What a Buyer Would Pay Today

Sometimes you do get an offer for your shares before an exit, through a secondary sale in a later round, a buyback or a private buyer. These offers are almost always well below the headline, because the buyer takes on the same gaps you face and wants to be paid for it.

body.label: Discount for lack of marketability
body.context: Secondary buyers of early-stage startup shares commonly ask for a meaningful discount to the last round price, and for plain equity shares in a company with a large preference stack, that discount can be very large. Late-stage, in-demand companies can sometimes trade close to or even above their last round.

children.text: Institutional investors face the same question when they report the value of their holdings. SEBI requires AIFs to have their investments valued periodically by independent valuers, and different funds can hold very different values for the same startup at the same time, as the Swiggy markdowns in Lesson 2.1 showed.

body.title: Taxes, fees and carry: the last gap

children.text: Even a real cash exit is not all yours. For Indian residents, based on the rates in force at the time of writing:
Long-term capital gains.
Unlisted shares held for more than 24 months are taxed at 12.5% without indexation, plus applicable surcharge and cess.
Short-term capital gains.
Unlisted shares held for 24 months or less are taxed at your slab rate.
Fund and syndicate economics.
If you invested through a SEBI-registered angel fund or syndicate, carried interest, commonly around 20% of profits, plus any fees, comes out before your share is distributed.

Example: in the big exit, Meenakshi receives ₹7.5 crore on a ₹20 lakh investment held for over 24 months. Her gain is ₹7.3 crore, and 12.5% tax on that is about ₹91 lakh before surcharge and cess. Had she invested through a fund charging 20% carry on profits, roughly ₹1.46 crore more would have gone to the fund manager first.
The Income-tax Act, 2025 applies from 1 April 2026. Confirm current rates and provisions with a chartered accountant before planning any sale.

body.title: Why equity is worth less
body.question: A startup raised its latest round at ₹1,000 per Series B CCPS. Why might a fair value for its plain equity shares be well below ₹1,000?
options: Equity shares have a lower face value than CCPS
The Series B price reflected liquidation preference and protections that equity shares do not carry
SEBI caps the value of unlisted equity shares
body.explanation: Investors paid ₹1,000 for a bundle of economics and rights, including getting their money back first in a disappointing sale. Equity shares sit behind that preference, so in many outcomes they receive less per share. Face value is irrelevant to worth, equity shares do vote, and SEBI sets no such cap.

body.title: Name the discount
body.textWithBlank: The discount a buyer applies because private shares cannot be easily sold is called a discount for lack of ___.
body.explanation: Often shortened to DLOM, it compensates the buyer for tying up money in an asset with no ready market.

body.title: The ₹60 lakh offer
body.scenario: A late-stage investor in UrbanNest offers to buy Meenakshi's entire 0.5% stake for ₹60 lakh in cash, closing within a month. Her friends say she would be "throwing away ₹1.4 crore" compared with the ₹2 crore headline value.
body.prompt: How should Meenakshi think about the offer?
body.modelAnswer:
Her friends are comparing the offer to the wrong number. ₹2 crore is the headline, not a price anyone will pay.

1. Compare with a realistic estimate. Her rough present value was about ₹48 lakh. A ₹60 lakh cash offer is above that estimate, and 3x her ₹20 lakh cost.
2. Test her assumptions. If she believes the big exit is much more likely than 20%, or will come sooner, holding could be worth more. If she thinks UrbanNest faces tough times, ₹60 lakh looks better.
3. Consider a partial sale. Selling part of the stake, for example enough to recover her ₹20 lakh cost plus tax, would lock in a gain while keeping exposure to the big exit.
4. Check the mechanics. Are transfers permitted under the Articles and shareholders' agreement? Do other investors have a right of first refusal? Is the buyer resident or non-resident, which brings in FEMA pricing?
5. Account for tax. If held over 24 months, the gain is long-term capital gains on unlisted shares. If the price is below the Rule 11UA fair market value, check Section 50CA and the buyer's position too.
6. Think about her portfolio. If this one stake is a large share of her net worth, reducing concentration has value beyond the arithmetic.

An offer below headline is not automatically a bad deal. Compare it with a realistic value, not a flattering one.

body.title: Estimate what your stake is really worth
steps: Note your share class and fully diluted percentage, and whether you hold equity or CCPS.
Find the total liquidation preference that sits ahead of your shares.
Sketch three to four exit outcomes with rough probabilities, including a shutdown.
For each, work out whether preference holders take their preference or convert, and what reaches you.
Calculate the probability-weighted value and discount it back to today.
Subtract expected tax and any fund carry or fees.
Use this range, not the headline, when judging any secondary offer or planning your finances.

cards.definition: Your fully diluted percentage multiplied by the latest post-money valuation. The most optimistic view of your stake.
The value lost by equity holders when preference holders are paid first in a sale.
The sum of each possible payout multiplied by its probability.
A future amount discounted back to today for time and risk.
Discount for lack of marketability: the discount a buyer demands for private shares that cannot be easily sold.
A fund manager's share of profits, commonly around 20%, taken before investors receive their share.
Gains on unlisted shares held over 24 months, taxed at 12.5% without indexation plus surcharge and cess, under the rates in force at the time of writing.

points: Headline valuation × your percentage is a ceiling, not a price anyone will pay today.
Five gaps separate paper from pocket: instrument, preference, liquidity, time and risk, and tax and fees.
In sales below a certain value, preference holders are paid first, and equity holders can lose far more than the fall in valuation.
Estimate value with a few realistic exit outcomes, weight them by probability and discount back to today.
Secondary offers usually sit well below headline. Judge them against a realistic estimate, not the headline.
Tax, fund carry and fees reduce the final amount, so include them before planning around any exit.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or valuation advice. UrbanNest and the individuals described are fictional, and all probabilities, exit values and discount rates are illustrative assumptions. Tax rates reflect rules in force at the time of writing and may change. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a chartered accountant before acting.
